books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, D. The Women's Rights Movement

stimulus.text:
"We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal; that they are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights; that among these are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. . . . He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise." — Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls, New York, 1848

The "Roll of Honor" listing the signatures to the Declaration of Sentiments is shown below.
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from the Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls, New York, 1848. Wording checked against the Wikisource text and the National Park Service transcript of the Report of the Woman's Rights Convention; ellipses mark omissions. Roll of Honor image viewed before writing: printed 1848, Library of Congress, public domain.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from the Declaration of Sentiments (1848), with its Roll of Honor
stem: The "Roll of Honor" shown here lists the signatures to the Declaration of Sentiments. The roll best supports which of the following claims about the convention?

options.text: The declaration was signed only by the men at the convention
options.misconception: The visible list is headed 'LADIES' and names Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton.

options.text: Women who signed put their names publicly to equal rights
The declaration was signed in secret to avoid newspaper publicity
options.misconception: A printed roll of honor publishes the names; secrecy would hide them.

options.text: The declaration was signed by members of Congress in Washington
options.misconception: The signers were reformers from New York, not congressmen.

rationales.A: The image shows a list headed 'LADIES,' beginning with Lucretia Mott. Women signed first and in large numbers.
rationales.B: The roll prints the signers' names under the convention's title, with Mott and Stanton at the top. Signing publicly meant owning the demand for equal rights.
rationales.C: A 'Roll of Honor' is printed to be seen. The names were published, not hidden.
rationales.D: The signers were women and men of the reform networks around Seneca Falls, not members of Congress.
rationales.general:
1. Read the heading. This is a roll of honor, a published list of signatures.
2. Read the names. Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton head the ladies' list.
3. Ask what signing meant. In 1848, putting your name to women's equality was a public act.
Background: One hundred women and men signed the Declaration of Sentiments at Seneca Falls.
Remember: a signature list is evidence of courage — ask what the signers risked by signing.
